title: By their grace I won
hook: in praise of his Sikhs he writes that by their grace he won battles and gave gifts (Khalsa Mahima)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shabad Hazare: a love song from the wilderness, and a straw bed better than mansions. Your line was ten hymns. Which one did you play? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-six.

Three words, said again and again, like a drumbeat. Inhi ke prasad. They close one phrase and open the next, so the poem never gets far from them. The poet is Guru Gobind Singh, the Guru his Sikhs followed. The poem is known as Khalsa Mahima, the praise of the Khalsa. And the three words point not upward to him, but outward, at the people who followed him: everything I have, I have through you.
screen: `CREDIT USUALLY FLOWS UP.` → `KHALSA MAHIMA.` → `EVERYTHING I HAVE, THROUGH YOU.`

segments.voice: The poem's lines are built on one repeated phrase: inhi ke prasad. By their grace. Paraphrased, it runs: by their grace I won battles. By their grace I gave gifts. By their grace my troubles were cut away, and by their grace my house is full. Otherwise, he says, there are countless poor ones like me. Hear the word prasad. It's the same word Sikhs know from the Mool Mantar's closing, gur prasad, by the Guru's grace. Normally grace comes from the Guru to the Sikh. Here the Guru turns it around and says grace has come from the Sikhs to him. That's not false modesty. Tradition sets the poem at a moment when someone questioned why the Guru gave so generously to his Sikhs, and this is his answer: they are worth it, because what I am, they made. It fits the Khalsa he formed. Tradition remembers that after he initiated the first Khalsa, he asked them to initiate him in turn. The teacher stood in line behind his students. Khalsa Mahima puts that same picture into verse. And look at what he lists. Not only victories. Gifts. A full house. The ordinary goods of a life. He traces them to people, not to his own skill. For Sikhs, the line sits underneath a habit visible in gurdwaras: the sangat, the community, is treated with deep respect, and this poem is one reason Sikhs give.
screen: `INHI KE PRASAD: BY THEIR GRACE.` · `GRACE TURNED AROUND.` · `THE TEACHER IN LINE BEHIND HIS STUDENTS.` · `THE SANGAT, HONORED.` · then, large: `BY THEIR GRACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank the people who carried you. Settle, and breathe. This time, don't start with one person. Start with a circle: a family, a team, a congregation, a group of friends, the neighbors on your street. Bring the whole group to mind, the way the Guru looked at the whole Khalsa. Then name what that circle has given you that no one member could have: a table to sit at, a place to belong, people who noticed when you were gone. With each gift, say silently, by their grace. If you pray, you can hold the whole circle before Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
By their grace I won. In Khalsa Mahima, Guru Gobind Singh says that by his Sikhs' grace he won battles, gave gifts and has a full house. Today's word.
screen: `BY THEIR GRACE I WON — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: by their grace. Today, give something back to the circle from the sit: an hour, a meal, a hand with a chore, the way the Guru gave to his Sikhs. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite and sing the Khalsa Mahima swayyas of Guru Gobind Singh, especially at gatherings about the Khalsa, and its refrain is often recalled when speaking of the respect owed to the sangat.

fork.setup: someone asks why you, the Guru, give so generously to your Sikhs. what do you answer?
options: because I am the Guru and it's mine to give.
because everything I have, I have by their grace.
fork.reveal: in Khalsa Mahima he answers with a refrain: by their grace I won battles, by their grace I gave gifts.

original.note: Gurmukhi: grace. the same word as gur prasad in the Mool Mantar; here, by their grace.

trapdoor: what you thought: a leader being polite about his followers.
what it means: by their grace I won, gave and have a full house. grace flowing from the Sikhs to the Guru.
what a scholar hears: prasad, the word of the Mool Mantar's gur prasad, deliberately turned around.

notes: The Khalsa Mahima refrain is paraphrased (battles won, gifts given, troubles cut away, house full, 'otherwise there are countless poor ones like me'); please check against the text. The text's number word (karor) is rendered 'countless' on purpose.
Tradition of the setting (someone questioning the Guru's generosity to his Sikhs, often told as a priest at a ceremony) is kept general so no community is cast as the foil; please confirm.
The Guru receiving amrit from the Panj Piare after initiating them is given as 'tradition remembers'.
Gurmukhi ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ and the link to gur prasad: please confirm the spelling as it appears in Khalsa Mahima.

Editor pass: new hook built on the refrain itself (the old 'credit flows up' opening, the trace-your-helpers practice and the thank-one-person carry repeated days 1228 and 1229); practice now turns to a whole community, as the poem does, and the carry is giving back rather than thanking; 'the first five' became 'the first Khalsa' and 'owed it everything' was softened.
